reason: The run is almost uniform on "endurance" (30 of 31 verses), a consistent departure from the traditional "patience", but Romans 2:7 has "perseverance". Mainstream translations split this word between endurance, perseverance, steadfastness and patience, so separate chapter runs could easily drift. An entry locks in the run's choice and states the one condition under which "perseverance" is allowed.
sense: holding out under hardship, opposition or delay; steadfast staying power

alternates.when: The word governs a genitive naming an activity one keeps on doing rather than a hardship one bears, as in Romans 2:7 (perseverance in good work), where "endurance of good work" would be unnatural English.

rationale: In period usage, including the Septuagint, the word means active staying power under pressure: standing one's ground, not giving up. Modern English "patience" suggests calm waiting or an even temper, which misleads; James 5:11 shows the problem, since Job protests loudly yet holds out. "Endurance" conveys the sense, keeps the word distinct from μακροθυμία (rendered "patience", and paired with it in Colossians 1:11 and 2 Timothy 3:10), and matches the verb ὑπομένω, "endure".
standard_view: The KJV has "patience" almost throughout. Modern versions abandon it but divide: NRSV and CSB mostly use "endurance", NIV and NASB often "perseverance", ESV often "steadfastness", and some use "patient endurance" in Revelation. The standard lexicons gloss it as endurance, perseverance, fortitude or steadfastness, so the default is within the mainstream.
